$schema-note: The register of RULE BLOCKS that more than one repo in the fleet carries verbatim.
Every repo's CLAUDE.md is a one-line `@AGENTS.md` include, so AGENTS.md is not reference
material an author consults when they remember to — it is the instruction file loaded into
every agent's context, in that repo, on every session. Two repos carrying different text for
the same rule therefore means agents BEHAVE differently per repo, silently.
Before this file existed the fleet upheld that by prose ('everything there applies here
unchanged') and by hand-carrying edits. MeshWeaver.Plugins#705 measured what that produced.
The gate that reads this file is .github/scripts/check-shared-rules.py.
ADDING A BLOCK: wrap the region in every listed repo with the markers, add the entry here,
and land it as ONE change set. The gate fails RED for a repo that is listed and has no
markers, so a half-landed adoption cannot be mistaken for a pass.

note: Both are HTML comments, so both are invisible in every rendered view and may sit on their
own line or inline. Block markers usually take their own line; an END marker placed
mid-sentence is the right move when a sentence's tail is role-specific — see this
register's conserve-work-products entry, where the block deliberately stops after the date
stamp and the clause after it stays outside.
Slot markers mark the spans that are legitimately per-repo — the checker replaces each with
the token <<name>> before comparing, so the slot's CONTENT is free while its NAME and
POSITION are asserted like every other byte. An EMPTY slot is legal and meaningful: it
records that this repo says nothing where another says something.
Comparison is byte-for-byte after exactly ONE normalisation: markdown soft-wrap is
collapsed (runs of whitespace, newlines included, become a single space). That is not a
loophole, it is the removal of one: core hard-wraps its AGENTS.md prose at ~200 columns
and the satellites at ~95, so a raw byte compare would encode each repo's wrap width as
part of the rule and be red on day one for a difference no reader can see. Everything a
reader CAN see — wording, punctuation, emphasis, links, emoji — is compared exactly.

a proposal — it is what the seven files already say about themselves (measured 2026-08-30):
• AUTHORING rules -> Systemorph/MeshWeaver.Plugins. Manufacturing, SocialMedia and
Reinsurance each open with 'The authoritative authoring rules live in MeshWeaver.Plugins'
AGENTS.md … Everything there applies here unchanged'; Education names the same file for
'the authoring rules for plugins … this file carries the content-authoring subset'.
• PLATFORM / PROCESS rules -> Systemorph/MeshWeaver (core). The conserve-work-products
block says so in its own text, in all six satellites: 'the platform rule lives in

So MeshWeaver.Plugins is a HUB for authoring and a SPOKE for platform, which is why 'is the
Plugins repo the hub for everything?' (#705 question 1) has no single answer: the hub is a
property of the BLOCK, not of the repo. Hence `hub` below is per-block.
`hub` takes a repo, or the literal "peers". "peers" means the listed repos must agree with
each other while no canonical home has been decided yet — it freezes an existing agreement
against further drift WITHOUT pre-empting where the rule should eventually live. It is the
honest encoding for #705's problem B (sections replicated across satellites with no canonical
home): those need a maintainer decision, and until it is made, 'they must not diverge further'
is a claim the gate can hold and the maintainer has not had to make.

why: Maintainer directive, 2026-09-04: 'everyone should use rest'. The occasion was an agent
polling `gh pr view` every 5 s, which exhausted GitHub's SECONDARY rate limit for the
whole session — every concurrent agent lost GitHub access, not just the one polling.
The rule is in a shared block rather than each repo's own prose because the failure is
FLEET-WIDE by construction: the limit is per USER, so one repo's watcher takes down every
other repo's session running as the same identity. A per-repo rule cannot express that,
and a repo that never adopted it would keep taking the others down.
Why the diagnosis is in the text and not just the prohibition: `gh api /rate_limit` reads
a pristine 5000/5000 remaining, 0 used while GraphQL is refused. Anyone who checks the
quota concludes they are NOT rate-limited and looks elsewhere — two agents did exactly
that on the day this landed. The pairing IS the signature, so it is stated.
No slots: the rule is identical everywhere, including the REST endpoints, because the
GitHub API is the same API from every repo. Core carries one extra sentence OUTSIDE the
block (its merge-queue paragraph keeps `dequeuePullRequest`, which REST cannot express) —
that is why the block names the merge queue as the reserved exception rather than
forbidding GraphQL outright, which would have been false guidance.
Adopted text-first: the six satellites landed the block before this manifest entry, so
the gate was never red on a half-finished rollout (Plugins#1317, Education#268,
Reinsurance#161, SocialMedia#137, Manufacturing#51, Memex#179).
The maintainer directive of 2026-08-30, hand-carried into all seven repos as core#2732,
Plugins#954, Education#236, Reinsurance#122, SocialMedia#111, Manufacturing#34 and
Memex#149. Seven PRs, no mechanism: nothing would have caught a repo being missed, and
nothing would catch one drifting afterwards. It is this register's first entry because
it is the worked example of the gap.
Slots, measured across the seven copies rather than assumed:
• doc-home — where THIS repo's durable form lives (core's Documentation tree, a node
repo's module folder, Education's course Space, Memex's docs/). The declared delta.
• reach — core alone adds 'and to the portal; the doc tree ships with the platform',
which is true of core and of no satellite. EMPTY in the other six, which is a legal
slot value and is asserted as such.
The block deliberately ENDS at 'Maintainer directive, 2026-08-30' — the date stamp is the
cheapest way to spot a stale copy, so it is inside the compared region — and the clause
after it is outside, because it states the reader's ROLE (core: 'this rule holds in every
repo of the fleet'; satellites: 'the platform rule lives in MeshWeaver's AGENTS.md') and
is correctly different at each end of the same pointer.
Byte-identical in these three node repos on 2026-08-30, and present in NEITHER hub in this
form (core and Plugins both carry a longer, differently-worded worktree rule). That is
exactly #705's problem B: spoke-to-spoke copy-paste with no canonical home.
`hub: peers` freezes the agreement that exists today without inventing a home for it. If
the maintainer later promotes this text into a hub, change `hub` to that repo and the same
gate starts enforcing the direction of inheritance instead of mere sameness.
Maintainer directive, 2026-09-17, verbatim across three messages: 'the grain keeps serving
old state until we send dispose request' / 'write this prominently in all repos' / 'in pull
request skill etc'. The occasion was a session that told the maintainer a dispose 'wouldn't
help' and was corrected — which is the whole reason the rule is stated rather than assumed:
the failure has no signal of its own. A per-node hub answers promptly and answers the OLD
thing, so it reads as a bad fix rather than as an un-recycled activation.
It is a FLEET rule and not a core one because the addresses that go stale are the ones the
satellites author: a NodeType's Source/*.cs, a layout area compiled in the mesh, node content
shipped in a bake. A satellite author who never reads this concludes their merged change did
not work. Core carries the framework half (RecycleNode, the off-router seam, HandleDispose's
root refusal); every repo carries the consequence.
One slot, `reference`, for the same reason never-hand-roll-ui has one: core links its own
Documentation tree and .claude/skills paths, which do not exist in the spokes; the spokes
point at the same page on the mesh as an absolute URL.
Landed hub-first in three steps, per SharedRuleBlocks.md: (1) core wraps its copy and
registers the block with `required-in` naming only the hub — green on its own, and the id
becomes known; (2) the six spoke copies; (3) `required-in` widened to all seven.
Landed: step 1 core#4641; step 2 Plugins#2050, Education#351, Reinsurance#220,
SocialMedia#205, Manufacturing#101, Memex#409; step 3 this entry's widening. Crm#127
carries the same text, unregistered — see the paragraph above.
Systemorph/MeshWeaver.Crm is deliberately NOT here. It is absent from `repos` above, so this
gate never reads it, and adding it is a separate change: it would require the read-only
fleet-reader App to be installed there AND Crm to carry every block already registered, and
an unreadable repo is a RED here by design. Crm carries this block's text anyway, so a later
registration is a one-line change rather than a rollout.
Maintainer directive, 2026-09-15: 'please refactor to use platform layout. see also in all the
Agents.md that we make clear to always use this and not create own ui frameworks'. The occasion
was Essentials/OperationRequest's approval screen: a Stack with inline CSS and the script as
Controls.Html(<pre>) collapsed to a sliver (a scroll container in a definite-height flex column
loses its content-height floor, the trap Store's hero hit in Plugins#1192) and every block had
a different width. Core had the rule; the six other repos did not, so an agent there never read it.
One slot, measured: `reference`. Core's 'Full reference' line links repo-relative paths
(.claude/skills/gui, the Documentation tree) that do not exist in the spokes, and Memex's
'Documentation links resolve' gate checks AGENTS.md links. The spokes point at the same docs on
the mesh (Skill/layout-area, Doc/GUI/LayoutAreas, Doc/GUI/DataBinding) as absolute URLs.
Rolled out hub-first, NOT satellites-first: this checker refuses any marker whose id the
register does not declare, and it reads all seven repos, so six spokes landing before this entry
would have reddened every core pull request until core merged. Step 1 registers the block with
`required-in` naming only the hub (green on its own, and the id becomes known); step 2 lands the
six spoke copies; step 3 widens `required-in` to all seven.
